turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on through, we'll grab a peak flow before the doctor sees you. Feet flat, big breath in, then blast it out hard as you can.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep. Give us a sec, I'm puffed just from the stairs, the lift's out again, which is very on brand for this place.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): No rush. Whenever you're ready.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. How'd that go?
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Three hundred and ten. Have another go, really empty out.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): My cousin did one of these at the chemist and it told him he was elite, which is hilarious, the man considers walking to the servo exercise.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Ha. Again, please.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, that felt better. Chest is whistling though, can you hear it?
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Yeah, bit of a wheeze. That one was three hundred and forty. One more, we take the best of three.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Last one. I swear these things hate me.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): Three hundred and twenty. So best is three forty. Sats are ninety seven percent, pulse is eighty eight. I'll leave it up for the doctor.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Is three forty bad? I'm twenty four, not a grandpa. My mate who plays footy reckons his is six hundred, but he's built like a fridge.
[SEG0013] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor'll put a number on what it means for you. Grab a seat, she won't be long.
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi, I'm Dr Nguyen. I've got your best peak flow at three hundred and forty, sats ninety seven, pulse eighty eight. What's been going on?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Wheezy. Had a cold, then the chest joined in. Worse when I laugh, which is tragic, because my flatmate will not stop sending me dog videos.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did the wheezing actually kick off?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, the cold was, I want to say, about a fortnight back. The wheeze, I can't pin the day. Maybe a week, maybe a bit longer. I wasn't writing it down.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or feeling properly crook, shakes, that sort of thing?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah, no temperature. Checked on the ancient thermometer at home, normal. I'm just tired, and the cough won't quit.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): What comes up when you cough? Any green or yellow, or any blood?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Dry, mostly. Bit of clear gunk in the morning, nothing colourful, no blood. It's that tickly one that keeps me awake, then I'm on my phone, which is stupid, I know.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Is the wheeze there all the time, or does it come and go?

[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Comes and goes, but most evenings it's there, and laughing or the stairs at work set it off. I shelve books at the library, so it's not exactly hard labour, but those stairs are steep and I have to stop halfway.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with it, or waking up gasping?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. It does wake me, around two, coughing and wheezing. I sit on the edge of the bed and hit the puffer. Not gasping like I can't get a breath at all, just miserable.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): Tell me about the puffers. Which ones have you actually been using?

[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Blue one and the brown one, and I always mix them up. I figured the brown one's the emergency one, darker, more serious looking, so I've been hitting the brown one maybe five, six times a day when I'm tight.

[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me stop you — the blue one is the reliever, salbutamol, the Ventolin, for when you're wheezy. The brown one is a preventer steroid, every day, not a rescue. Sounds like you've had them backwards.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, classic me. Wait, no, I have been on the blue one heaps too, two puffs a go, whenever the brown doesn't fix it. So it's the blue one, two puffs, maybe five or six times a day. The brown one I grab when I panic, two puffs, but I'm not doing it every morning like I'm meant to.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's alright, we'll untangle it. Do you know the strength of the brown one, the micrograms?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Label's rubbed clean off. Could be a hundred micrograms, could be two hundred. I turfed the box months ago.

[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the preventer's not really being taken, and the reliever's up around five or six times a day, which is too much. Ever been in hospital with your breathing, or had steroid tablets before?

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No hospital. A GP in Brisbane a couple of years ago said mild asthma and gave me the puffers. Never had the tablet steroids. Moved down in January and just kept using whatever was rattling around in the bathroom drawer.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or vape?

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Never smoked. Flatmate vapes on the balcony and it stinks, but I don't. I have a few drinks on the weekend, nothing heroic. Tried a run on Sunday and a bloke walking a greyhound lapped me after one block, which I'll be recovering from emotionally for a while.

[SEG0036] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a listen, big breaths. Scattered wheeze both sides, a little louder on the right, and no crackles. You're talking in full sentences, not distressed. Heart sounds are normal, nothing extra.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the right side's the tight one. Is that grim? My uncle popped a lung once from coughing, he brings it up every Christmas like it's a party trick.

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Worth knowing about your uncle, but that doesn't sound like you today. Thinking out loud, this could be the asthma flaring after the virus or just twitchy airways after the cold, and I wouldn't call it pneumonia or a pneumothorax — no fever, clear sputum, no crackles, sats are good, wheeze both sides. Working impression is an acute flare of your asthma off the back of that cold. I'm not locking in anything more serious, and I don't need a chest film to say that today.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): So not dying. Excellent. Do I need antibiotics? Mum's convinced antibiotics fix weather.
[SEG0040] person_3 (DOCTOR): No antibiotics. Doesn't look bacterial. What I do want is a short course of steroid tablets to settle the flare, and we'll fix how you're using the puffers.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Tablets, hey. Will I go weird? I read they stop you sleeping, and I'm already up half the night with this.

[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): They can make you a bit hungry, restless, maybe more awake, just for these few days. Prednisolone by mouth, fifty milligrams, once every morning, for five days. The tablets are twenty five milligrams, so that's two with breakfast. Don't take extra if you miss one.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Two of the twenty fives, with breakfast, no doubling up. What do I do with the blue one, keep smashing it?

[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Blue salbutamol, two puffs when you're wheezy, and if you're still needing it more than four times a day after a couple of days I want to hear about it. Brown preventer, two puffs morning and night, every day, not just when you panic. If you can't read the canister, take it to the chemist to identify it, or bring it to me.

[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Morning and night even if I feel fine. Chemist's the one by the servo on Burke Road, the bloke knows my name, which is either wholesome or a sign I buy too many heat packs.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Either way. No chest x-ray today. If you get more short of breath, or a fever, or the wheeze hasn't eased after the five days, then we'd get one.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): And if I'm just sort of the same, not worse?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Book a review in one week regardless, so I can recheck the peak flow and actually see the puffer. Reception will fit you in. If things slide before that week, don't wait.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): One week, or sooner if I slide. The rehearsal dinner's Saturday, pizza at my sister's, not the actual wedding. Am I allowed pizza and people?
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): If you can walk and talk comfortably, go to the dinner. Skip the running. If you can't finish a sentence or your lips go blue, that's emergency, not a wait-and-see.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Blue lips, can't talk, emergency. Pizza yes, running no. Do you do medical certificates? Work's precious about sick days and I literally alphabetise fiction.
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll do a certificate for today and tomorrow. Rest, fluids, and start the prednisolone this morning if you've eaten. I'll see you in one week.
[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): Legend. Thanks. If the greyhound asks, I was conserving energy.

spec.situation: Teenager or adult wheezy after a cold; confuses blue and brown inhaler; uses the reliever 'maybe five, six times a day'; peak flow numbers read by the nurse. Doctor adds a steroid course.
features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

omissions.text: Negative finding omitted: no smoking history but exposure to second-hand vape from flatmate who vapes on the balcony.
Past treatment history omitted: patient has never had steroid tablets before.
Medication detail omitted: prednisolone tablets are 25 mg each, so the prescribed 50 mg dose is two tablets with breakfast.
Medication side-effect counselling omitted: doctor advised prednisolone can cause increased hunger, restlessness, and feeling more awake for the short course.
Examination detail omitted: patient was talking in full sentences.
Examination detail recorded incompletely: doctor said heart sounds were normal, nothing extra, not just 'added heart sounds absent'.
Assessment detail omitted: doctor considered but did not think this was pneumonia or pneumothorax today.
Plan detail omitted: doctor said no chest x-ray is needed today.
Follow-up purpose omitted: review in one week was specifically to recheck peak flow and inspect the inhaler/puffer.

omissions.text: The cough is mostly dry but produces a small amount of clear sputum/gunk in the morning.
Cold/viral illness started about a fortnight before the consultation.
No shaking/rigors or feeling 'properly crook' were reported when asked about fever/shakes.
The patient reports nocturnal waking around 2 am with coughing and wheezing and sits on the edge of the bed to use the inhaler.

There was medication misuse/confusion: the patient had the blue and brown inhalers mixed up and thought the brown inhaler was the emergency inhaler; the doctor corrected that blue salbutamol/Ventolin is the reliever and the brown inhaler is a daily preventer steroid.
The brown preventer inhaler was intended to be taken every morning, but the patient is not doing that.
Moved down in January and has just been using inhalers left in the bathroom drawer since then.
Second-hand vape exposure is from the flatmate vaping on the balcony; the patient themself does not vape.
The doctor's differential included 'just twitchy airways after the cold' in addition to an asthma flare after the virus.
The doctor advised no antibiotics because it does not look bacterial.
If still needing the blue inhaler more than four times a day after a couple of days, the doctor specifically wants the patient to get in touch.

If the wheeze has not eased after five days, or if shortness of breath worsens or fever develops, chest x-ray would be considered; this was linked to deterioration or lack of improvement after the steroid course.
The one-week review was advised regardless, not only if symptoms persist or worsen.
Emergency advice included: if unable to finish a sentence or if lips turn blue, this is an emergency rather than wait-and-see.
Prednisolone was to be started that morning if the patient had eaten.
